correctness.rationale: The asymptotic proof is correct. A word that is a product of two palindromes is exactly a cyclic reflection-symmetric word. Reflection fixed sets have size on the order of \(2^{m/2}\), and primitive symmetric words have a unique reflection, yielding \(\Theta(m2^{m/2})\) symmetric words. Every symmetric word is a palindromic periodicity, while every length-\(n\) palindromic periodicity has a symmetric period of some length \(m\le n\), so \(S_n\le a_n\le\sum_{m\le n}S_m\), which gives \(a_n=\Theta(n2^{n/2})\) and exponential growth rate \(\sqrt2\). I independently enumerated all binary words through \(n=14\), reproducing both the package palindromic-periodicity counts and symmetric-word counts.
residual_risks: The proof gives order of growth, not a sharp leading constant or full asymptotic expansion.

originality.rationale: The final asymptotic is implication-covered by prior results. The exact enumeration of binary products of two palindromes/symmetric words is classical: Kemp's formula, as recorded in OEIS A007055/A284873 and revisited by Guo--Shallit--Shur, gives \(S_n=\Theta(n2^{n/2})\). Fici--Shallit--Simpson already characterize a palindromic periodicity as a word having a symmetric word-period and note that every symmetric word is one. Combining these two published facts immediately gives \(S_n\le a_n\le\sum_{m\le n}S_m\), hence the audited \(\Theta(n2^{n/2})\) statement. The fact that their paper asks the asymptotic question does not erase this direct prior implication under the audit bar.
residual_risks: The exact leading behavior of \(a_n\) itself may still be open; only the audited order-of-growth claim is judged covered.
